The Chinese Just Built a Rolls-Royce Fighter That Can Float and Tank Turn. Meet the Altior!
14 photos
Photo: BYD
The Chinese want to take a big bite of the European ultra-luxury brands' market share as well, and it looks like it is not more than they can chew. Quite the contrary! BYD has just unveiled the Yangwang Altior, and it looks ready to take on the Rolls-Royce Ghost and Phantom, along with the Mercedes-Maybach S-Class.
Meet the all-new BYD Yangwang Altior. It is the firm's ultra-luxury full-size flagship sedan, designed specifically to steal the show (and the market, too!) from established models such as the Rolls-Royce Ghost and Phantom or the Mercedes-Maybach S-Class in its home market, but also in Europe.
Unveiled at a black-tie event in Abu Dhabi, the United Arab Emirates, the sedan comes with innovative technology, extreme luxury, and staggering performance. Known as the Dingao in China, the model will be marketed as the "Altior" worldwide. That is the Latin word for "Higher," which clearly marks BYD’s intentions.
The model with an upright grille flanked by headlights with diamond-cut crystalline glass and suicide doors is 220.5 inches (5,600 millimeters) long, sitting right between the Rolls-Royce Ghost (212.6 inches/5,399 millimeters) and the Rolls-Royce Phantom (226.9 inches/5,762 millimeters), while it is 5.2 inches (131 millimeters) longer than the Mercedes-Maybach S-Class .
Photo: BYD It is 79.9 inches (2,030 millimeters) in width and stands 62.6 inches (1,590 millimeters) tall, while sitting on a wheelbase of 137.8 inches (3,500 millimeters). BYD hasn’t unveiled details about the weight of the massive sedan, but it is projected to weigh between 6,800 pounds and 7,100 pounds (3,084 kilograms and 3,220 kilograms).
The cabin features a four-seat layout which prioritizes rear passenger experience. It features rear reclining "zero-gravity" executive seats with multi-mode massage, heating, and ventilation. At the press of a button, the front passenger seat folds completely flat to give the rear passenger a completely unobstructed view ahead.
The cabin is wrapped in semi-aniline leather and displays authentic natural wood trim and pure wool carpets, along with hand-embroidered badging. A premium 39-speaker Dynaudio sound system and a 21.4-inch folding screen, which deploys from the headliner, provide entertainment for those on board the ultra-luxury sedan.
The BYD Yangwang Altior sits on the firm’s e⁴ Platform, shared with the U8 SUV and U9 supercar, and is powered by a quad-motor system, with each motor powering a wheel. The setup allows independent wheel torque vectoring, crab walking, and tank turning, and enables it to float across deep water in case of emergency, just like the U8 SUV , which is already on the market.
Photo: BYD BYD presents this as a strictly emergency safety feature, specifically designed to protect occupants in case the car accidentally ends up in deep water. Highly calibrated hull-depth sensors immediately detect when the vehicle enters water and loses contact with the road.
At this point, the onboard computer automatically raises the active suspension to its maximum height, shuts down the HVAC external intake vents, and tightly seals the windows and the panoramic sunroof to make the cabin temporarily watertight.
Because the four motors control each wheel completely independently, the Yangwang Altior uses the rotation of the wheels as makeshift paddles. By spinning the wheels on one side faster than the other, the e⁴ platform vectoring allows the driver to steer, turn, and navigate the floating vehicle back to land.
In the meantime, on land, the quad-motor powertrain pushes out a staggering 1,300 horsepower for a run from 0 to 62 mph (100 kph) in just 2.36 seconds. BYD hasn’t unveiled the top speed of its all-new Yangwang Altior, but it surely won’t hit 312.65 mph (503.17 kph) like the record-breaking Yangwang U9 Xtreme hypercar .
Photo: BYD The carmaker hasn't disclosed any details about the battery capacity that is installed in its ultra-luxury limousine, but we do know that it features BYD's second-generation Blade Battery pack, which can store enough energy for a drive of up to 621 miles (1,000 kilometers). Using BYD's ultra-fast megawatt-level "Flash Charging" technology, it can charge from 10% to 70% in approximately 5 minutes under optimal conditions.
The car sports an intelligent, active suspension, capable of scanning the surface ahead in real-time, micro-adjusting individual wheel dampers to filter out the imperfections of the road. The model also features what BYD calls the God's Eye System, an autonomous driving feature based on a cutting-edge 4-nanometer Schwanji A3 system chip.
The all-new BYD Yangwang Altior ultra-luxury sedan is expected to hit the market later this year with a starting price of roughly 2,080,000 Chinese yuan, which is the equivalent of approximately $311,500. That makes it cheaper in its home market than both the Rolls-Royce Ghost and Phantom, but more expensive than the Mercedes-Maybach S-Class.
The numbers make it a serious contender for the established ultra-luxury models both in China and Europe. The BYD Yangwang Altior is officially planned for a European launch, though buyers in Europe will have to wait a little bit longer to get their hands on one. The model has zero chance of officially setting wheels in U.S. land.

Maserati Celebrates the Ghibli's 60th Anniversary With Special Ghibli SS Classiche Certification
9 photos
Photo: Maserati
Although the Ghibli is no more, Maserati has found an interesting way to celebrate one of its most celebrated nameplates. Instead of commissioning a one-off build or coming up with a new concept, the Stellantis-controlled Italian manufacturer has turned its attention to a 1970 model that the Maserati family has kept in its own collection. The celebratory vehicle is listed as AM115/49*1948* by its maker.
Marking 60 years since the 2-seater concept was unveiled at the Turin Motor Show in November 2026, this model has recently passed through the automaker's classic vehicle certification process. AM115/49*1948* left Modena on November 25, 1970, and its first owner specified Oro Longchamps paintwork.
Today, said coupe wears fresh Giallo Fly paintwork. The cabin retains the original black leather upholstery, adding to the specialness of this VIN. Under the long and beautifully sculpted hood, the Giorgetto Giugiaro-penned fastback is rocking the larger 4.9-liter naturally aspirated V8 instead of the lesser 4.7-liter unit.
The Ghibli SS motor is related to the 4.7-liter mill, and this engine was key to creating the fastest Maserati road car at the time. Its top speed, according to Maserati, is 280 kilometers per hour (nearly 174 miles per hour). SS chassis numbers include the /49 designation, whereas AM115 stands for Ghibli.
Maserati produced the first generation in limited numbers through 1973, and the AM in AM115 designates a founding Maserati brother. Alfieri Maserati was the driving force behind the company. Unfortunately, this Maserati brother never fully recovered after a horrific 1927 racing accident. Alfieri died in 1932, at just 44 years old, from surgical complications while attempting to save his remaining kidney.
Photo: Maserati A serious grand tourer by 1970 standards, the Ghibli SS combined the ability to cover long distances at considerable speed with the comfort and quality expected from an expensive Italian coupe. Designed by Giugiaro during his tenure at Ghia, the Ghibli used dry-sump lubrication because Maserati wanted to mount its V8 as low as possible in the chassis.
The dry-sump lubrication system partly explains the design of the hood, with Giugiaro creating a very sleek front end with a remarkably flat and low hood. Commercial deliveries kicked off in 1967, and two years later, Maserati expanded the range with the Ghibli Spyder.
Fewer than 1,300 vehicles were produced in total, of which the Spyder accounted for 125. The SS coupe stopped production after 425 units, making the Maserati family-owned Ghibli SS all the more special. Beyond the Italian Republic, the Ghibli attracted plenty of attention from well-to-do peeps.
Henry Ford II comes to mind, for he bought a Ghibli that was displayed in the lobby of the Ford Motor Company's Development Center in Dearborn. Not exactly the Italian Riviera, but hey, it's something! Today's GranTurismo and GranCabrio both carry the first-generation Maserati Ghibli's philosophy into a different era, one that includes twin-turbo sixers and full-electric muscle.
The base GranTurismo is a very fast machine due to the all-wheel drive and a nicely calibrated ZF automatic box, with Maserati claiming 3.7 seconds to 60 miles per hour (97 kilometers per hour). Upgrading (or downgrading, depending on how you see electrification) to the Folgore specification means 751 zero-emission ponies and 2.6 seconds to 60 miles per hour. Mechanic Called To Revive Old Mustang Parked in Garage 14 Years Ago, It's a 1968 Shelby GT500
51 photos
Photo: YouTube/BeAircooled
“It all starts with a phone call about an old Mustang that needs some help getting back on the road.” Don’t they all? And, with millions of old Mustangs made in the moniker’s 62 years on assembly, it’s not even that exhilarating anymore. Except this old Mustang has had a few upgrades made to it before it was sold new. Some would argue it’s not even a Ford anymore, and they’d probably be right, because “S H E L B Y” is a funny way of spelling Ford, isn’t it?
Few childhood daydreams survive contact with adulthood, yet Brandon Cummings of the BeAircooled YouTube channel recently lived out the ultimate gearhead fantasy. As an 8-year-old boy gluing plastic valve covers onto a 1/25-scale Revell 428 model engine, and later as a 16-year-old teenager watching Steve McQueen pilot a Highland Green fastback in Bullitt, he never imagined wrenching on an identical 1968 Shelby GT500 inside his own Glenview, Illinois restoration shop.
The opportunity arrived through a casual phone call from a mutual buddy named Josh, who mentioned a friend named Chris looking to revive a dormant Mustang before putting it up for sale. Having wrenched on plenty of vintage Ford Broncos, trucks, and pony cars, Brandon agreed to help, only to learn that the sleeping machine was actually 1968 Shelby GT500 serial number 562, parked untouched in Chicago since late 2012.
Chris caught the collector car bug with a 1961 Ford Thunderbird convertible before seizing the chance to buy Shelby number #562 in the spring of 2001. Historical records revealed that this early-build 1968 fastback was originally ordered and delivered in late 1967 through JD Ball Ford in Miami, Florida. Over 25 years of dedicated ownership, Chris logged roughly 4,000 miles cruising strictly to local car shows around the Chicagoland area.
Photo: YouTube/BeAircooled During the first 12 or 13 years of his stewardship, Chris made the Highland Green muscle car a regular fixture at suburban gatherings. He hit Elmhurst on Wednesday evenings, Woodfire Chicken on Friday nights, Des Plaines on Saturdays, and Rand Red Hots whenever the weather cooperated. Once those weekly neighborhood cruise nights gradually dried up in 2012, he tucked the big-block pony inside his brick-and-timber city garage for 14 years.
Beyond driving the fastback locally, Chris spent the early 2000s traveling across America to attend Shelby conventions held at active racetracks, including Road America in Wisconsin, California Speedway in Rancho Cucamonga, Nashville, Raleigh-Durham in North Carolina, and the Volo Museum in Illinois. He met Carroll Shelby so frequently that the legendary Texan greeted him by first name, personally signing the dashboard above the passenger sea.
To preserve the car's originality, Chris fitted an aftermarket air cleaner lid over the Holley carburetor and carried the factory steel cover to the 30th Shelby American Automobile Club reunion in Riverside, California, in July 2005. There, both Carroll Shelby and Daytona Coupe racing driver Bob Bondurant autographed the original metal lid. Shelby also signed Chris's March 1957 Sports Illustrated issue celebrating his historic 24 Hours of Le Mans victory.
Photo: YouTube/BeAircooled The memorabilia archive accompanying number #562 even includes a hardbound book bearing 24 authentic signatures from key Shelby American pioneers. Alongside Carroll Shelby and Bob Bondurant, the pages feature autographs from project engineer Chuck Cantwell, team photographer Dave Friedman, surfboard shaper and fiberglass specialist Tweety, and Doyle Gammell, who worked as a teenager at Dean Moon's Speed Shop in 1962 installing the first Ford V8 into an aluminum AC Cobra.
Extracting the prized fastback from its long slumber proved urgent because Chris was preparing to demolish the aging wooden garage. With helpers bracing the fragile overhead door so it would not collapse onto the roof, Brandon guided the dusty green Mustang out into the Chicago daylight for the first time since 2012. A flatbed tow truck then hauled the time capsule to the BeAircooled shop for a thorough mechanical awakening.
Up on the shop lift, Brandon bypassed the temptation to crank the dry engine and started at the fuel tank beneath the undercoated chassis. After slicing the petrified outlet hose, he drained nearly 10 gallons of foul-smelling, yellow-tinted vintage gasoline that had soured over 14 years. Threading a borescope camera inside the tank revealed a spotless metal floor, clean upper baffles, and an intact sender float free of rust scale.
Photo: YouTube/BeAircooled Pulling all four cobweb-draped wheels exposed a braking system that demanded careful rejuvenation before taming a big-block Shelby on public streets. While the passenger-side rear drum was bone dry, a weeping differential axle seal had coated the driver-side backing plate and Ford-stamped shoes in sticky gear oil. Up front, green repaint overspray on the calipers and aging rubber lines prompted Brandon to send the entire hydraulic assembly to Phoenix Caliper.
While the front hydraulic disc brakes undergo restoration and the 428 V8 awaits an internal cylinder borescope inspection, number #562 stands as a proud monument to celebrated first-generation Shelby Mustang history. Spanning six model years from 1965 through 1970, the original lineage encompassed the small-block GT350, the track-bred GT350R, the Hertz GT350H rent-a-racer, the big-block GT500, the one-off 1967 Super Snake, and the mid-year 1968 GT500KR King of the Road.
Across that entire 1965 to 1970 first-generation run, total Shelby Mustang output reached 13,912 vehicles (including race, prototype, test mules, and preproduction examples). Annual production totaled 562 fastbacks in 1965, 2,378 cars in 1966, 3,225 units in 1967, and a peak of 4,451 vehicles in 1968, followed by 3,294 cars built for 1969, of which 789 unsold examples received updated 1970 vehicle identification numbers.
Photo: YouTube/BeAircooled Offered across four model years from 1967 through 1970, the GT500 line accounted for 7,184 units. That big-block tally comprises 2,048 fastbacks in 1967, 1,423 standard GT500s and 1,571 GT500KRs in 1968, and 2,541 GT500s across 1969 (1,872 copies) and 1970 (470 cars). Regular production body styles included two-door fastbacks, renamed SportsRoof in 1969, and two-door convertibles offered from 1968 to 1970, alongside two experimental notchback coupes.
Most of those were the iconic fastbacks (5,938), leaving 1,246 ragtops on the table. Irrespective of body style, all GT500s made in the classic era had a 428 cubic-inch big-block V8 underhood. The 1967 GT500 debuted with a 355-horsepower 428 “Police Interceptor” V8 and dual four-barrel carburetors.
The lone 1967 Super Snake packed a 427-cubic-inch V8 (it’s the sole exception to the 428 rule, although the 427 Side oiler was offered as an option on the GT500). Early 1968 GT500s used a single four-barrel 360-horsepower 428 Police Interceptor before the 335-horsepower 428 Cobra Jet and Super Cobra Jet powered 1968 GT500KRs and all the 1969/1970 models. Transmissions were available in 4-speed Toploader manual or 3-speed C6 automatic variants.
Photo: YouTube/BeAircooled Breaking down the 4,451 Shelbys built for 1968, Marti Auto Works records document 1,457 small-block GT350s, all powered by the 250-horsepower J-code 302-cubic-inch V8. That total splits into 1,053 fastbacks (including 224 automatic Hertz cars), with 445 manual 4-speeds and 608 C4 3-speed automatics, plus 404 convertibles comprising 214 manual 4-speeds and 190 C4 3-speed automatics.
Standard 1968 GT500 production with the S-code 428 Police Interceptor V8 reached 1,423 units: 1,020 fastbacks comprising 405 manual 4-speeds and 615 C6 3-speed automatics, and 402 convertibles with 153 manuals and 249 automatics. Finally, the R-code 428 Cobra Jet powered 1,571 GT500KRs, dividing 1,053 fastbacks into 530 manuals and 523 automatics, plus 518 convertibles with 267 manuals and 251 automatics.
Brandon, the YouTubing mechanic, will document the revival of #562 over several episodes, so stay tuned. As for Chris, the owner of the car, he’s getting ready to end 25 years of meticulous ownership. I’ll keep an eye out for this car, if it goes on public sale again. “Again,” as in it was sold at a Kruse auction in May of 1991, for $22,201. You tell me if that was a lot of money for a 1968 Shelby GT500 back then, but bear in mind that it’s Canadian dollars. At the exchange rate of the time, it was about $19,300 USD.

EICMA 2026 • Honda CRF1150L Africa Twin Enduro Sports Is a Tongue Twister, Weighs Less but Offers More
1970 'Cuda 4-Speed Rocks One of Mopar's Greatest Engines Ever, Owner Pampered It 50 Years Straight
93 photos
Photo: Hagerty Marketplace/EB_266fhv
Holding onto a classic muscle car for 50 years is a rare testament to devotion, transmuting steel and vinyl into a living family heirloom. In Dresher, Pennsylvania, a dedicated caretaker is finally parting ways with his 1970 Plymouth 'Cuda 340 coupe after half a century of continuous ownership. Currently offered at auction on Hagerty Marketplace, this vibrant Mopar carries 50 years of memories and 86,300 miles on its odometer.
Acquired around 1976 when E-body pony cars were affordable used transportation, this 1970 'Cuda escaped the fate of drag-strip abuse and backyard modifications that claimed so many of its peers. Its owner sheltered the coupe inside a garage for the entire 50-year span, preserving all of its original body panels and factory interior. It now heads to the auction block with a clean Pennsylvania title, its original build sheet, and a trove of spare parts.
Over those 50 years, maintenance remained honest and sympathetic to the car's factory character. The exterior was resprayed once in the late 1970s in its original FY1 Lemon Twist paint, paired with a black vinyl roof. Inside the black vinyl high-back bucket-seat cabin, the front carpeting was replaced, while a clogged vent drain from 50 years ago required a small floor patch between the parking brake and clutch pedal.
Aside from that decades-old floor repair, some minor paint flaws, age-related interior wear, and an inoperable N85 tachometer, the garaged coupe remains remarkably solid and rust-free. More importantly, it still runs and drives great using its numbers-matching 340-cubic-inch V8 and code-correct A833 4-speed manual gearbox. Stirring the gears through the iconic Hurst Pistol Grip shifter above the woodgrain-trimmed center console still delivers the visceral thrill it did in 1970.
Photo: Hagerty Marketplace/EB_266fhv The lineage behind this coupe began on April 1, 1964, when Plymouth launched the Valiant-based Barracuda fastback 16 days ahead of the Ford Mustang. After a 1967 redesign introduced notchback and convertible variants alongside the fastback, Plymouth unveiled the 340-cubic-inch LA-series small-block V8 for the 1968 “Formula S” package. In 1969, Plymouth adopted street slang to create the A56 'Cuda package, where the 340 V8 served as standard powerhouse.
The 340 V8 remained a staple of the Barracuda lineup for six model years, from 1968 through 1973, before the 360 V8 replaced it in 1974. Out of 180,529 Barracudas built for the United States market during that six-year window, 35,330 left the factory with a 340 V8 under the hood. That figure includes 3,917 Formula S 340 cars out of 45,412 Barracudas in 1968, and 6,018 340-powered A-body Barracudas out of 31,987 cars in 1969.
Within that 1969 tally, United States records specifically account for 1,839 Formula S 340 models and 652 A56 'Cuda 340 hardtops. Production of 340-equipped Barracudas peaked in 1970 with 9,018 cars out of 48,867 total units, split between 6,294 'Cuda 340 models and 2,724 Six-Barrel AAR 'Cudas. Thereafter, Plymouth built 3,440 'Cuda 340s out of 16,492 cars in 1971, 6,354 out of 18,490 in 1972, and 6,583 out of 19,281 in 1973.
Photo: Hagerty Marketplace/EB_266fhv For 1970, stylist John E. Herlitz penned an all-new E-body platform that erased every trace of the economy Valiant. The 48,867 Barracudas built for 1970 spanned three distinct series: 23,723 base Barracudas (22,336 hardtops and 1,387 convertibles ), 7,886 luxury Gran Coupes comprising 7,320 hardtops and 566 convertibles, and 17,258 performance 'Cudas made up of 16,710 hardtops and 548 ragtops. Only the 'Cuda and AAR 'Cuda offered the 340 V8.
Breaking down the 9,018 340-powered 1970 models further reveals just how special this Pennsylvania survivor truly is. All 2,724 AAR 'Cudas with the 290-hp 340 Six-Barrel were hardtop coupes, divided into 1,120 4-speed manuals and 1,604 TorqueFlite automatics.
Among the 6,294 4-barrel 'Cuda 340 cars, 6,032 were hardtop coupes—1,872 with the 3-speed manual, 2,372 with the 4-speed manual like this example, and 1,788 automatics—while just 262 were convertibles, including 19 3-speeds, 88 4-speeds, and 155 automatics.
Photo: Hagerty Marketplace/EB_266fhv Coded E55 on the fender tag (see the metal plate in the gallery, the 340-cubic-inch V8 featured a 10.5:1 compression ratio, a forged crankshaft, 2.02-inch intake valves, and a 650-cfm Carter AVS four-barrel carburetor. Factory-rated at 275 hp at 5,000 rpm and 340 lb-ft of torque at 3,200 rpm, the small-block propelled a 1970 'Cuda 340 with 3.55:1 gears from 0 to 60 mph in 7.5 seconds and down the quarter-mile in 15.0 seconds at 94 mph in period tests.
Across Chrysler Corporation in 1970, the feisty 340 V8 powered 56,672 vehicles from the Plymouth and Dodge divisions. Within Plymouth showrooms, besides the 'Cuda 340 and AAR 'Cuda, the 275-hp engine turned the compact Duster 340 into a budget weapon with 24,875 units built. Over at Dodge, the 275-hp 340 armed 13,785 Dart Swinger 340 hardtops and 6,633 Challenger 340 models, while the 290-hp 340 Six-Pack powered the 2,399 Challenger T/A coupes.
When ordered new at Dodge Main in Hamtramck, Michigan, this example started at a base price of $3,164, which included the J54 “Raising Bran” sport hood, and the standard 383 V8 (the big-block was regular equipment, while the small-block 340 came at extra cost).
Photo: Hagerty Marketplace/EB_266fhv Specifying the 340 V8 added $44.05, the 4-speed manual cost $195.25, and the Performance Axle Package with a 3.55:1 Sure-Grip 8.75-inch rear end, heavy-duty suspension, and 26-inch radiator added $102.75, while power drum brakes cost another $42.95.
The original buyer also checked boxes for the $89.90 62 Rallye instrument cluster, $196.25 AM/FM Multiplex stereo, $84.45 vinyl roof, $54.45 console, $39.65 light package with fender turn signals, $29.60 body-side moldings, $26.65 rear defogger, $17.85 drip rail moldings, and $14.05 paint, bringing the original sticker past $4,100. Now bidding at $25,000, this cherished 50-year companion awaits its next chapter – there are still ten days to go of this online bid.

EICMA 2026 • Triumph TF-E Bikes Get Even More Enduro With Updates for the 2027 Model Year
1970 Dodge Challenger R/T Flaunts Ultra-Rare Factory Option
16 photos
Photo: American Steel Classics/YouTube
Introduced in 1970, the Dodge Challenger was quite popular during its first year in showrooms; the company sold nearly 77,000 units in the US. However, this massive number hides quite a few rare iterations of the muscle car.
The Hemi version is the most obvious one. Only 356 cars were ordered with the 426-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) V8, a powerplant that turns the Challenger into a sought-after, six-figure classic. The R/T convertible is also rare, with only 963 examples made. This number includes all four powerplants that were available with the R/T model.
If we add the Special Edition (SE) package into the mix, we get a couple more R/Ts that have three-digit production numbers to brag about. Only 875 units were born with the four-barrel 440-cubic-inch (7.2-liter) RB, while 296 got the six-barrel variant of the same mill (also known as the 440 Six-Pack).
However, many other Challengers are rare due to certain options that weren't popular at the time, regardless of what they have under the hood. The R/T you see here, for instance, is not a convertible and was born with the base 383-cubic-inch (6.3-liter). It's one of 9,067 hardtops fitted with this powerplant, but it was also ordered with an option that we rarely see today.
At first glance, this Challenger R/T may seem a bit mundane. Yes, the four-speed manual transmission narrows its production number to only 2,720 units, but that's far from being in rare territory. But look close enough and you'll notice that it has a brownish roof. That's not a vinyl top; Dodge didn't even offer vinyl in that hue. What you're looking at is a painted roof.
In addition to a color-keyed top and the optional vinyl roof, the Challenger was also available with a so-called "two-tone paint" feature. The latter allowed customers to choose a roof color that was different than the main body hue. The option added the code V02 on the fender tag, and, needless to say, this Mopar has it. So it's not some sort of day-two mod.
How rare is the two-tone paint option? Well, Dodge did not keep detailed records, but Mopar experts agree that it's a super-rare option. And we can get a better idea by looking at the 1970 Challenger T/A registry: only two of the over 1,000 units documented have the V02 feature. This means that only four or five R/Ts fitted with the 383/four-speed combo may have been specified with two-tone paint.
But the precise figure is a bit irrelevant here. This Mopar is most likely a one-of-one classic due to its color combo. The original owner went with a very unique Go Mango body with a Burnt Orange roof. He also opted to pair the interior with the top color. You probably won't see another one out there.
The Challenger is waiting for a new home at American Steel Classics, a Mopar-focused dealership in Celeste, Texas. It's a "nicely restored car" with a numbers-matching drivetrain. Both the suspension and the engine have been rebuilt, with the latter sporting Hooker headers and an Edelbrock carburetor. It has all-original sheet metal except for the center of the trunk floor.
How much to take this two-tone beauty home? Pricing is a fixed $95,000 . That's a lot of dough for an R/T with a standard engine, but likely worth it to the right people due to the rare paint option. What do you think?

EICMA 2026 • Trio of New Morbidelli T802 Motorcycles Will Make Short Work of Every Surface
The c.fold Transformable Travel Trailer Is Designed to Be Different in Every Way
21 photos
Photo: YouTube/Clever Campen
It's always a shame to see a nice concept not get the chance to get off the ground and move into production as a "real" product, for whatever reason. That feeling of regret also comes with the new c.fold travel trailer, despite the fact that it was never meant to go into production in the first place.
The c.fold travel trailer is a transformable trailer from German specialist Dethleffs, one that was ironically never meant to move past the concept stage. It's a real product, though, and it's getting real miles in the real world, pushing the envelope on travel trailer design and introducing innovative features to EV towing.
The c.fold was introduced earlier this year at the 2026 edition of the CMT trade show in Stuttgart, as the latest iteration in a series of concepts that Dethleffs is doing on the future of RV-ing . These are basically RVs, both towables and motorhomes, that the company designs and builds for an imagined future, with features that may or may not trickle down into actual production series models.
It's a fully functional prototype, designed for real-time use by a pair of experienced RV-ers who want to use it with their new electric vehicle (EV). Perhaps a more accurate description would be that it's a one-off conceptual vehicle meant as a testbed for innovative features and design.
Photo: Dethleffs Semantics aside, the c.fold is a neat piece of engineering and RV design – and more details about it have just come to light. That's because the owners and Dethleffs have agreed to let an established RV publication to take it out for a test drive to confirm its reduced impact on range and enhanced drivability. You can see that test drive in the video tour at the bottom of the page.
First things first, though.
The c.fold was created by Dethleffs for Monika and Peter Marchart, a pair of longtime Dethleffs customers who wanted something built specifically for their new EV.
Photo: Dethleffs The solution proposed was a transformable caravan, one that would travel compact in road mode but would expand at camp to offer all the basic creatures for the travelers, including light cargo hauling capabilities, some autonomy, and the basic features like a bathroom, a galley kitchen, and a nice bed.
In the process, though, Dethleffs pretty much rewrote every rule in book. They started with construction with honeycomb aluminum panels (Alucore) in two layers, placing between them an insulating layer of recycled PET plastic. On the inside, they added a layer of felt, which also helps with creating a cozier vibe.
Arguably the biggest innovation was the decision to use independent wheel suspension and air suspension, designed specifically for the project by partner Goldschmitt. The c.fold is the only caravan in Europe to feature this kind of suspension, and the recent test drive shows that the difference it makes on the road is incredible.
Photo: Dethleffs Then, Dethleffs opted against using a trailer chassis on which to mount this structure. Instead, the base is overlapping Alucore panels, which means that the axle is bolted directly onto the floor – onto the almost fully enclosed underbelly, to be more precise.
This, the very low-profile design in road mode, of just 1.65 meters (5.4 feet), and an dry weight of under 1,000 kg (2,204 lbs), ensures an easy towing experience. The exterior design obviously also plays an important part in that: the c.fold has rounded corners and a tapered rear end, which means reduced drag.
Dimensions include a width of 1.9 meters (6.2 feet) and a length of 5.49 meters (18 feet), with a height at camp of 2.18 meters (7.15 feet). That means that, inside a caravan that's exceptionally lightweight, surprisingly light profile, and so easy to tow, you get full standing height. You also get almost 400 kg(882 lbs) of payload capacity , which is way more than you get with most European caravans.
Photo: Dethleffs That said, Dethleffs promised with the c.fold a travel trailer that would not severely impact the range of the electric towing vehicle, and they delivered. Clever Campen, who conducted the test drive on a VW ID.4 GTX test car with a 77kWh battery, reported an impact on range of 22.4 kWh per 100 km/62 miles, as compared to 36 kWh per 100 km with a traditional caravan.
The test drive video doesn't show the inside, but the second one included below, of the display unit in Stuttgart, will have you covered for that.
The interior of the c.fold is as interesting as the exterior design , with modular furniture of real wood, hinged so that you can even have overhead cabinets that you don't have to remove when you go back on the road, plenty of space to move around, lots of natural light, and an overall very cozy vibe.
Photo: Dethleffs One of the many downsides of this type of transformable trailers is that they almost always have an improvised or half-baked quality about them, but the c.fold is able to avoid that.
It also comes with features like 300W of solar on the roof, mounted perfectly flush in the name of the same principles of aerodynamics, a 300Ah lithium battery pack, a 2000W inverter, and a scale feature integrated into the air suspension, so you can always see on the app just how much payload you still have to work with. The folding out mechanism is fully automated, taking under 1 minute to fully set up.
Photo: Dethleffs The Dethleffs c.fold isn't meant for mass production, but based on the positive reception of the concept , it's probably safe to assume at least some of the great things about it will make it into other series production models – in one form or another.

8 November 2026
Watch the episode on YouTube and subscribe so you never miss an update!

In this week’s News in Brief, we look at the latest developments shaping global shipping and air cargo, from growing port congestion concerns to shifting capacity and geopolitical uncertainty.
The Loadstar managing editor Gavin van Marle joins us fresh from the World Ports Conference in London to discuss the key talking points from the event, the latest concerns around potential disruption at the Los Angeles and Long Beach ports, and what the return of container services to the Suez Canal could mean for shipping rates and congestion. We also examine why the transpacific trade remains so lucrative for carriers.
Then, new TIACA director general Mammen Tharakan joins us to discuss the air cargo market, including tight capacity and strong demand on the transpacific, the potential impact of returning Middle Eastern capacity, and how ongoing instability around the Strait of Hormuz is affecting market confidence and contracting decisions.
From port disruption and Suez transits to the air cargo capacity crunch, we bring you up to speed on the stories driving the freight industry this week.

context_references.quote: “Forefront Concept … demonstrates the contribution that Renault Group’s industrial and technological expertise can make to a strategic sector such as unmanned ground vehicles with multiple applications expected across both civilian and military sectors in the years to come,” explains François Provost, CEO, Renault Group. “This innovative project brings together two complementary areas of expertise: Renault Group’s in the rapid, large-scale and cost-effective development and production of high-performance, reliable technological products and John Cockerill’s in the defense industry.”

source_document.body:
Forget what your Fox News -addicted uncle told you about cheese-eating surrender monkeys. The French military has centuries of storied military victories and traditions behind it, and Renault wants in on that action with a new, autonomous electric vehicle platform designed to tackle the Armée de Terre’s most demanding missions.
Co-developed by the EV experts at Renault Group and the defense experts at Belgian electronics firm John Cockerill, the new Forefront concept previews a new, modular ground vehicle that can be rapidly industrialized at a controlled cost, with unique mobility and off-road performance, and capable of autonomously navigating complex terrain. The result is a machine that could front-line logistical capabilities for both defense and civilian applications, enabling missions to be carried out remotely in very high-risk and hard‑to‑reach environments.
“Forefront Concept … demonstrates the contribution that Renault Group’s industrial and technological expertise can make to a strategic sector such as unmanned ground vehicles with multiple applications expected across both civilian and military sectors in the years to come,” explains François Provost, CEO, Renault Group. “This innovative project brings together two complementary areas of expertise: Renault Group’s in the rapid, large-scale and cost-effective development and production of high-performance, reliable technological products and John Cockerill’s in the defense industry.”
Money is money
Forefront at work; via Renault.
Renault is quick to point out that its new concept isn’t just suitable for military work. Although it’s worth pointing out that the Renault-provided image, above, isn’t just AI slop: it would be impractical if it was real, with no real obvious way to get those RCP pipes on or off the thing. That said, presenting their military killbot as a construction mule is at least more credible than the “ ambulance ” and “ troop transport ” use cases we’ve seen touted by similar concepts on the American side.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Forefront seems to be little more than a rendering at this stage, with the first of the Forefront concept prototypes set to take part in a number of exercises and trials in the months ahead to further refine the concept.
